nodes.title: The tools
nodes.text: How the SpecSheriff tools carry out the base of the guidelines.

children.title: Where the files are
children.text:
Each domain of the specification is kept under `specs/<domain>/`, opening with its header in `specs/<domain>/00-<domain>.json`, contracts under `specs/contracts/`, the technical appendix under `specs/tech/`, each of its sections in a file of its own — a domain's in `<domain>.json`, the stack's in `stack.json`, the technical debt's in `debt.json` — and the guidelines under `specs/_guidelines/`: a project's own guidelines in `project.json`, and, in the repository the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in, the base in `spec.json` and the appendix of the tools in `tools.json`, which every other project reads from the plugin of its agent (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5, §s-2pdy9gw2jrjvfb4). A part divided into one file per section keeps its files in its directory.

The schema is kept in `specs/_schema/` of the repository the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in, and every other project reads it from the plugin: `node.schema.json` for a node and its metadata, `section-file.schema.json` for the file of a part, and `extension.schema.json`, the schema of an extension. A project's extension of it (§s-eferktypcj7njt5) is kept in `specs/_schema/project.schema.json`, validated against the schema of an extension and read together with it (§s-xzcw3hv4hmxz7h7); any other file another project keeps under `specs/_schema/` is refused as a copy of the schema.

Confirmations are kept in `specs/_confirmations.jsonl`, the archive of removed nodes in `specs/_archive/<name>.json`. `specs/_viewer/` (the map) and `md-version/` (the readable export) are rebuilt after every change to the specification and not stored in git.

The SpecSheriff tools provide the command `sheriff`. In a terminal it is run from the tools a plugin keeps on the machine (§s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p), as `node <tools>/dist/cli.js`, `<tools>` being the data directory of the plugin for Claude Code or the `tools/` of the plugin for Codex CLI in Codex's cache.

Their plugin for pytest, the package `pytest-specsheriff`, is installed by pip from the branch `release`: `pip install "pytest-specsheriff @ git+https://github.com/non4me/SpecSheriff@release#subdirectory=skills/pytest-specsheriff"`.

The settings of the SpecSheriff tools that a project shares are kept in `sheriff.config.json` at the root of the repository; those of the reviewer's runs, which each user confirms, are kept in the user's git configuration (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u). Among them, glob patterns name where the system's code lives and where its tests live: the code is read for tags, the tests for the sids they declare, and a file neither names for neither — which is how the repository's configuration, its own tools and their tests are kept out of the system's code by where they live (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc). Among them, too, are the command that runs each check and each generator the project's own guidelines add (§s-2fau85dfyyeq66m, §s-km4x4s26kv7pjze), and, for each, the glob patterns naming the files of its code and of its tests (§s-utf4mbt7ref8g9c). The repository the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in says so by the setting `"writesSpecSheriffGuidelines": true`.

The documents are the markdown files the repository keeps outside `specs/`. The tools of the specification are the files of the SpecSheriff tools: a project keeps only the files `sheriff init` writes, and the repository the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in keeps them under `skills/`, where the tests are read for the sids they declare.

The specification's owner is the one the top node of `project.json` names; the levels its domains stand at are the members of the list carried by the rule of `project.json` that refines §s-nkyty4dy9x2v2a4; the rule that puts the specification live is the rule of `project.json` that refines §s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2; and the files kept as fixtures of tests are those named by the glob patterns the rule of `project.json` refining §s-6hha5en226aj8hu lists.

decisions.problem: The toolset SpecSheriff provides was spelled the toolset, SpecSheriff's toolset and the tools: three names for one thing, the first a general word that does not say whose.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it is named the SpecSheriff tools.

decisions.problem: No package installed the command `sheriff` any more: an agent found the SpecSheriff tools through the plugin for Claude Code, and a person's terminal had no command at all.
decisions.ruling: The owner: nothing new is built. In a terminal the command is run from the copy of the tools the plugin keeps in its data directory, whose path is the same on every machine; the agent's skills run it from the tools the plugin carries.

decisions.problem: `pytest-specsheriff`, installed by pip, does not follow the plugin for Claude Code when Claude Code updates it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: nothing is built and no rule says how it is updated. It registers the mark, checks its form and opens the reported name with the sid, while the checks read the sid from the test's source, so an older copy breaks no check; updating it is a person's action, which the practitioner's guide gives.

decisions.problem: By the owner's rule of 2026-10-29, what only the repository the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in does leaves the guidelines for an internal document; this rule says where that repository keeps the guidelines, their schema and its tools, and what it is not read for.
decisions.ruling: The owner: those clauses stay. They say what the SpecSheriff tools do in a repository that writes the guidelines, which every project's copy of the tools carries out; the procedures only that repository runs — a release, the build, running its own plugin — are in its internal document.

decisions.problem: The rule kept every setting of the SpecSheriff tools in sheriff.config.json, which every clone shares, while the settings of the reviewer's runs are each user's to confirm (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u).
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u: the settings of the reviewer's runs are kept in each user's git configuration rather than in sheriff.config.json.

decisions.problem: A project's own schema was refused as a copy, and nothing said where a project's extension, the commands of its checks and generators, the rule putting it live, or its records of history and fixtures are kept.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the extension is `specs/_schema/project.schema.json`; the settings name the commands of a project's checks and generators; the rule putting the specification live and the lists of records of history and fixtures are rules of `project.json`, the tools reading those files from the lists rather than from the settings, so each is said once.

decisions.problem: The rules of how each check is made (§s-4kd2pave7vm4hmd), confirmed by the owner that day, name what this node did not say.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying those rules out: the schema of an extension, the settings naming the code and the tests of each project's own check and generator, the repository's own tools and their tests exempt from tags, no special exemption of the SpecSheriff tools' files from the check of locations.

decisions.problem: The system's code came to include its tests, which carry a sid rather than a tag.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-hheus6f395ynqvc: the repository's configuration, its own tools and their tests are kept out of the system's code by where they live.

children.title: The commands
children.text:
`sheriff validate`, `sheriff binding`, `sheriff citations`, `sheriff guard`, `sheriff message` and `sheriff review` implement the checks as the rules of §s-4kd2pave7vm4hmd describe them.

`sheriff init` sets a repository up for the SpecSheriff tools, and `sheriff remove` takes SpecSheriff out of it (§s-7unxytshhc4md54).

`sheriff reindex` gives a sid to every node that has none, computes every node's location from where it is, empties every incoming list and rebuilds it from the outgoing ones, rebuilds the index in every domain's header from the domain's sections, writes, beside each field of type one of, the values gathered for it from elsewhere in the specification, each with the sid of the node it comes from (§s-ju5vcanbjph7mgh), and empties the status of every checked node outside the SpecSheriff guidelines the project takes unless the latest line for its wording's fingerprint is a confirmation by the node's owner; it is run after every change to the specification.

Before anything else, `sheriff reindex` renames, in every file of the specification and of its archive, each key and value an earlier release of the SpecSheriff tools wrote under another name: the key `id` to `location`, the key `rationale` to `reason`, and the kind `record` to `recordType`. A renamed key keeps its place among the node's keys. A field of type one of whose own list an earlier release wrote empty, which then stood for the values the domains add, takes those values as its source instead.

Then `sheriff reindex` merges, in every file it rewrites, the values an object holds under one key, each into those written before it: two lists into one holding the members of the first and then those of the second that the first does not hold, two objects key by key in the same way with each key where it was first written, and two values JSON Schema holds equal into one. It names every key it merged, with the file and each value's line, and refuses any other two, naming the file, the key and each one's line and value, and then writes no file.

`sheriff confirm` records an owner's confirmation (§s-v4qus7raqnwzneb).

`sheriff export` writes the readable export in markdown, one file for each file of the specification, each node as §s-k4nqjr96ux7a5m7 says.

`sheriff render` writes the map, the mindmap of the specification's structure drawn from its nodes (§s-rpv4fkdqqguptqd).

`sheriff guide` prints every node of the guidelines — the base, the appendix of the tools and the project's own — as §s-k4nqjr96ux7a5m7 says, and the figures counted off the model as it prints: how many nodes each part holds and how many of them are checked.

`sheriff show` prints a node, found by its sid or its location, as §s-k4nqjr96ux7a5m7 says.

`sheriff model` prints as JSON the model of the specification where it runs: every node as its file holds it, with its location, the part and the file it stands in, and the owner named nearest above it. A project's own check or generator is handed it on its standard input (§s-2fau85dfyyeq66m, §s-km4x4s26kv7pjze).

`sheriff todos` prints, as text, every item of the todos of the specification where it runs, the archive left out, and the SpecSheriff guidelines too where the project takes them. The items come the newest first, those of one day in the order the specification reads. Each comes with its date, who its author is, what is to be done, and the sid, location and title of its node (§s-t28j22vbdmmeqnh).

`sheriff types` generates, from the RecordTypes, the types and the runtime checks of the system's code, where the technical appendix says they stand, and the files each generator the project's own guidelines add prints, run by the command the settings name for it and handed what `sheriff model` prints on its standard input, printing as JSON each file's path, its content and the sids of the nodes it is written from (§s-km4x4s26kv7pjze). It writes a file only where the file is missing or holds, line endings aside, anything other than what it generates, and names each file it writes. Where the check of generated copies refuses the list of those files or a RecordType (§s-dbk2vyeg8z5jxna), or a project's generator ends with an exit status other than zero, it names each refusal and writes no file. It writes a file only once every node that file is generated from is checked, and names each node it waits for:

- the types and runtime checks wait for every RecordType;
- a file a project's generator prints waits for the nodes it is written from and for the rule listing that generator.
children.reason:
The reindex rewrites whole the files written by hand, so it keeps everything they hold: two values written under one key are each somebody's intent, kept together where both can stand and refused where keeping one would drop the other, since nothing says which was meant; and every merge is named, because one of them may have been written to replace the other.

`sheriff types` runs after every edit an agent makes and at every commit, where the pre-commit hook copies each file it names into the working tree for its author to stage (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw): the files it names are then exactly those its author has to stage, and a file whose content no edit changed keeps its modification time, so that nothing watching the files takes it for changed. Line endings are set aside because git may check a file out with endings other than those committed, which would make every file differ at every run.

Where anything is refused, no file is written, so that nothing a failed run generated reaches the code. Each refusal is named, so that whoever runs it, by hand or through a hook, learns which node or list to change. Each file waits only for the nodes it is generated from, so that a node awaiting confirmation holds back no file generated without it.

Handed the model rather than left to read the files, a project's check or generator finds nodes by their location, finds owners and follows links as the tools do, in whatever language the project writes it; a generator prints its files rather than writing them, so that they are written, compared and held back on the same terms as the types.

A project's files are written by the release that wrote them, so a release that writes something in another form rewrites it where the files are next read, and the project rewrites nothing by hand.

decisions.ruling: The owner: sheriff types writes a file only where its content changes, names each file it writes, and writes nothing where anything is refused; the checks are implemented as the table describes them; the map is named as the mindmap of the specification's structure; each command stands in a paragraph of its own, sheriff init before sheriff reindex.

decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j: code generated from the nodes waits until every node it is generated from is checked, no commit changing it meanwhile, and its lag is reported.

decisions.problem: A project's own checks and generators had no way to read the model, the values gathered beside a field had nothing writing them, and nothing gave the model to a program outside the tools.
decisions.ruling: The owner: `sheriff model` prints the model as JSON, handed to a project's check or generator on its standard input; `sheriff types` writes the files a project's generator prints, on the terms of the types; the reindex writes the gathered values; which command runs a project's checks is said in the table of how each check is made.

decisions.problem: No command listed the work put off on the nodes, kept in their todos.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's rule on work put off (§s-t28j22vbdmmeqnh): `sheriff todos` lists every item, the newest first, each with its node.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

decisions.problem: The owner renamed a node's id to location, its rationale to reason and the kind record to RecordType, while every project's files and confirmations hold the old names.
decisions.ruling: A technical consequence in the owner's name: the reindex renames them in every file once.

decisions.problem: Earlier releases wrote an empty own list for a field whose values the domains add, while a field now names its one source.
decisions.ruling: A technical consequence of the owner's rule on one source for a field's values, in the owner's name: the reindex gives such a field the values the domains add as its source.

decisions.problem: `sheriff types` wrote no file while any RecordType, any node a project's generator writes from or any rule listing a generator was unchecked, while the check of generated copies held each kind of copy to its own nodes: a generator's file confirmed while an unrelated RecordType waited could be neither written nor committed.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's rule that what is generated waits for the nodes it is generated from (§s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j): each file waits only for its own nodes, here and in the check of generated copies (§s-dbk2vyeg8z5jxna).

children.title: Setting a repository up and taking SpecSheriff out of it
children.text:
`sheriff init` sets a repository up for the SpecSheriff tools. It writes the git hooks into `.githooks/` (§s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p); stages with the executable mode, 100755, each hook there that holds what it would write and that git's index does not already hold with that mode, naming each one, or, where it cannot stage a hook, names it and says how to stage it executable; and turns them on.

For the agent `--agent` names, `claude` or `codex`, `claude` where the option is not given, `sheriff init` adds the marketplace and the plugin to `.claude/settings.json` as a project declares them (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5), keeping every other key there, or writes the agent's hooks for Codex into `.codex/hooks.json` (§s-n76wt2bkqdmh78x), keeping every other hook there. It refuses another name, naming the two it takes.

Where they are missing, `sheriff init` writes a `sheriff.config.json` naming no file as code or tests, and a `specs/_guidelines/project.json` naming as the specification's owner the email git is configured with; where the repository keeps no file in a language the SpecSheriff tools read for tags, that `project.json` also holds, unchecked, the rule "The specification is live", whose text is "This project's specification is live.", refining §s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2. It replaces a hook or a declaration that holds what an earlier release of `sheriff init` wrote, naming each, and no other file that differs from what it would write, naming each one instead; so run again it changes nothing. A hook or a declaration holds what an earlier release wrote where, line endings aside, it equals one of the texts the earlier releases wrote, which the SpecSheriff tools keep.

Where the repository's hooks ran from elsewhere before, from `.git/hooks/` or from another folder `core.hooksPath` named, `sheriff init` names each hook found there, git's samples aside, and says that it no longer runs until it is moved into `.githooks/<hook>.d/` (§s-n4m5zvh96yb299p).

`sheriff remove` takes out of a repository what `sheriff init` writes outside `specs/`, for both agents: each git hook, the marketplace and the plugin in `.claude/settings.json` and the agent's hooks for Codex in `.codex/hooks.json`, where each holds what `sheriff init` writes now or wrote in an earlier release; `core.hooksPath` where it names `.githooks`; a key left holding nothing, a file left holding no key, and `.githooks/`, `.claude/` or `.codex/` where that leaves it empty; and `sheriff.config.json`, whatever it holds. It leaves each hook and declaration that differs, naming it, and leaves `specs/` as it is, naming it. It stages nothing, and run again it changes nothing. `sheriff remove` names each folder `.githooks/<hook>.d/` it leaves, and says that the project's own tools in it no longer run.
children.reason:
On a system whose files keep an executable bit, git runs a hook only where its file has the bit, and a clone checks a file out with the mode its commit records. Git takes that mode from the file when it stages it where files keep the bit, and records it as not executable where they keep none, as on Windows, where git runs a hook whatever its mode; so a hook set up there would reach the clones unable to run, and nothing on the machine that set it up would show it. A mode reaches the clones only staged and committed, and git stages a mode only with the file's content, so `sheriff init` stages the hooks it holds and nothing else: what else a commit holds stays its author's choice.

Claude Code reads its plugin from `.claude/settings.json` and Codex its hooks from `.codex/hooks.json`, so `sheriff init` writes for the agent the project is set up with, and a project moving to another agent runs it again for that one. A hook or a declaration written by an earlier release is the tools' own, so it is replaced; one that differs otherwise was changed by hand and is the project's.

The settings `sheriff init` writes name no code yet, so whether a project starts with code is read from the files the repository keeps in the languages the tools read for tags. The rule is written unchecked, since only its owner confirms a node (§s-67vekyup7y8smap).

`sheriff remove` takes out what `sheriff init` writes and no more. `sheriff.config.json` goes whatever it holds, because a repository holding it is one the plugins act in (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5) and its settings serve only the tools; `specs/` stays, being the project's own content. What `sheriff remove` takes out is in git's history, and what a commit holds stays its author's choice, so it stages nothing.

Taking up the method moves where git looks for hooks, so a hook the repository ran before stops running unless it is moved, and `sheriff init` names each one rather than moving a file of the project. Taking the method out unsets that place again, so the project's own steps stop running with the checks.

children.title: Building the map
children.text: `sheriff render` reads the nodes and writes into `specs/_viewer/` a web page that draws the map from them. The web page draws it with markmap, from an outline in markdown that the command builds and keeps nowhere. The page carries markmap and every library it needs, each with its licence notice, and loads nothing from the network. Nothing is written by hand at any step: the map is regenerated from the nodes exactly as the readable export is.
children.reason:
The nodes are already a structure any drawing tool can read, so the map keeps no format of its own between them and the web page: a kept format would be a second copy of the structure, and one that keeps only titles and nesting, dropping the sids, status and links that anything shown on top of the map would be bound to.

The specification is worked on wherever its repository is, often without a network; carried with the page, the drawing needs none there, as the export needs none. The libraries' licences ask that every copy keep its notice.

children.title: What the export, the guide and `sheriff show` write of a node
children.text:
`sheriff export` and `sheriff show` write a node with every value its file holds for it. They write each link with its type, its direction, its ratio where it holds one, and the sid, location and title of the node at the other end.

`sheriff guide` writes each node of the guidelines as the export does, except its metadata.

Each of them writes a value that is not text, other than its links and its children, under its key as JSON, but for two. A rule's list any of whose members is an object (§s-v7vd4ydrwexsgsj) has its other values written as JSON and its members as a table: a column for each property a member holds, the one the list names first and the others in the order they first appear, and a row for each member, a primitive member in the first column alone; a cell holding a list or an object holds it as JSON on one line, a `|` escaped. The values gathered beside a field of type one of are left out of the JSON and written after it as a list under the field's name, each with the sid, location and title of the node it comes from. The export and the guide write a node's children after it, each under a heading one level deeper than its parent's; `sheriff show` writes the node alone.
children.reason:
A person reads the specification in the export, since a structure a schema checks is hard to read (§s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j), and a person or an agent reads one node through `sheriff show`. A value either leaves out, such as a RecordType's fields, a rule's list or a decision taken on the node (§s-gqbj8849rf224qa), is one its reader never learns of and works without. A sid alone tells a reader nothing of the node it names.

An agent reads the guide whole before it works on the specification, to follow the guidelines: it needs each node as it binds, its links included, since a link may exempt a rule from implementation or narrow it. The metadata serves whoever changes a node, who reads it whole through `sheriff show`; written into the guide, it would only lengthen what every agent reads.

JSON is the form the file already holds a value in, so its reader learns no form of its own for it. The export and the guide keep the tree of the file they are written from, while `sheriff show` is asked for one node.

Written as JSON, a list of objects spreads each member over lines and repeats every property's name, so its members are hard to compare; a table puts each member on one row and each property down one column. The file names a gathered value's node by its sid alone.

children.title: The hooks
children.text:
Each check lives in a command a git hook calls: `.githooks/pre-commit` runs `sheriff export` and `sheriff render`, then `sheriff validate`, `sheriff binding` and `sheriff citations`, and last `sheriff types`; `.githooks/commit-msg` runs `sheriff message` and then `sheriff review` on the file git hands it; and `.githooks/pre-push` runs the tests of the system's code and of the project's own checks and generators by the command `sheriff.config.json` names as its `testCommand`.

A clone turns them on with `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`, which the `SessionStart` hook of the agent, the plugin's for Claude Code or the project's for Codex (§s-n76wt2bkqdmh78x), runs where `core.hooksPath` is unset, saying so, and reports where it names another directory. The `SessionStart` hook also names each git hook in `.githooks/` that git's index holds without the executable mode and, on a system whose files keep that bit, each whose file lacks it, and says how to make each one executable on every system — `chmod +x <hook>` and `git update-index --chmod=+x <hook>`, then a commit — changing neither the mode of a file nor git's index.

The `SessionStart` hook of the plugin for Claude Code writes into the git configuration of the user, by `git config --global`, each setting of the runner `claude` (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u) the user has given as an option of that plugin (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5), wherever the configuration lacks it or holds another value. Where the git configuration lacks a setting of the runner `sheriff review` would take at a commit in the repository (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u, §s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p), the `SessionStart` hook of either agent names each such setting, with the default `sheriff review` takes for it, and asks the agent to offer the user each default to confirm or replace and to write with `git config --global` the value the user answers, the default included. It asks so once for each runner on each machine, and marks it asked in the git configuration, as `specsheriff.review.claudeAsked` or `specsheriff.review.codexAsked`; where the mark stands it asks nothing.

At a commit, the checks read what is staged, written out to a directory of its own and read there against the repository's history, while the export and the map are written in the working tree, a failure to write them reported and stopping nothing. Whatever the checks found, `sheriff types` then runs in the directory the staged files are written out to; the pre-commit hook copies each file it writes there into the working tree, in place of what stands at the same path, and stages none of them, and what `sheriff types` refuses stops the commit.

Before a push, the pre-push hook compares the working tree with the commit each ref the push creates or updates names, directly or through a tag, leaving aside the files the working tree ignores. Where a file differs between them, stands in only one of them, or stands in the working tree without having been added, it refuses the push, naming each such file; otherwise it runs the tests in the working tree.

The agent's hooks are Claude Code's, which the plugin for Claude Code declares (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5), and Codex's, which `sheriff init` writes into the project (§s-n76wt2bkqdmh78x): before an edit made with the file tools or with `apply_patch`, `sheriff guard` judges it. After such an edit or a shell command (Claude Code's `Bash` or `PowerShell`), where the last commit or the working tree, the files it ignores left aside, differs from what the hook noted in the clone's git directory once the checks last ran, or nothing is noted, the checks run over the working tree, its difference from the last commit read as the commit: first, where a file under `specs/`, `sheriff.config.json` or a file the settings name as the code of a project's own generator differs, `sheriff reindex`, `sheriff export`, `sheriff render` and `sheriff types`; then `sheriff validate`, `sheriff binding` and `sheriff citations`. What they refuse is reported to the agent, and so is each node whose status `sheriff reindex` emptied.

An edit made through the shell is not judged before it is made, nor is a file `sheriff types` writes after an edit; the checks after them and at the commit still read them.
children.reason:
A hook runs each check where the commit is made, so that none depends on whoever commits remembering it; kept in the repository and turned on by one setting, the hooks are the same in every clone.

The agent's hooks come with the plugin for Claude Code and with the project for Codex, so that every clone's agent is held by them; and they turn the git hooks on, so that no clone's gate depends on its user remembering to.

The checks read the working tree against the last commit, so where neither changed since they last ran they would find what they found then; the reindex, the export, the map and the types are made from `specs/` and `sheriff.config.json` alone. Run only where a change can bear on them, they hold up no session reading the repository through the shell; compared with where they last ran, a change made between calls, by a command left running or by hand, is checked at the next call. A node whose status the reindex emptied waits for its owner again, and an agent not told goes on as if it were still checked.

On a system whose files keep the executable bit, git skips a hook whose file lacks it, printing a hint and refusing nothing, so a commit there passes no check while the hooks are on. The session start reaches every clone, those where the git hooks are skipped and so cannot report among them, and every repository whose hooks were committed or staged again without the mode. It leaves the mode to the author, since a mode changed in the working tree alone is a difference the pre-push hook refuses, and recording it in the index is staging, which is the author's choice.

The settings the reviewer runs at are a choice of what the user pays, so only the user makes it (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u), and they make it once, when they install the plugin, as they decide to take the plugin itself, so that no later session is interrupted by it. Claude Code asks for a plugin's options when it enables the plugin and hands them to the plugin's own components, while the git hooks that run the reviewer run outside Claude Code; so the plugin's session start writes them where the git hooks read them, in any repository, so that a project set up later finds them there, and wherever they differ, so that a change the user makes to them reaches the reviewer. Codex asks nothing for a plugin it installs, and its agent's hooks stand in the project (§s-n76wt2bkqdmh78x), so the first session in a repository taking the method is the earliest its user can be asked; a user Claude Code enabled the plugin for without asking is in the same case. A hook cannot ask the user anything, so it has the agent ask. The question is put once, its mark keeping it from being put again, since a setting left unanswered is named at every review it costs (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u). Only the runner that would run is asked for, since a user is asked only about what they will pay for.

The types and runtime checks generated from the RecordTypes are generated after every edit an agent makes and at every commit, so that they follow the nodes at the first edit or commit after every node they are generated from is checked (§s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j), and a person who edits the nodes without an agent has no hook between edits. At a commit they are generated from the staged nodes, because a commit is judged only by what it holds (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh): what `sheriff types` refuses there is a fault of that commit, and the copy it writes is the one that commit has to hold.

At a commit it runs after the checks, so that they read what is staged rather than a copy the hook wrote, and whatever they found, since the check of the generated copies is among them and refuses exactly the commit whose copies it writes; after an edit it runs before them, so that they read the copies the edited nodes produce rather than report ones about to be replaced.

The copy goes to the working tree, since the directory the commit is written out to is gone once the hook ends, and the author stages from the working tree; it replaces whatever stands at that path, since a generated copy is never edited (§s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j).

What a commit holds is its author's choice, so the hook stages nothing; a commit holding a copy left behind nodes that are all checked still does not pass, since the check at the commit comparing each kept generated copy with what the staged nodes produce refuses it until its author stages the new one.

A failure to write the export or the map stops no commit, since the commit holds neither, and every check reads the commit being made and never what it does not hold (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh).

A test run judges a commit only where the files it reads are those the commit holds, since every check reads the commit being made and never what it does not hold (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh). The tests run in the working tree rather than in a copy of the commit, because they need what each checkout installs or builds for itself, which a copy of the commit lacks.

The files the working tree ignores are left out of the comparison of the working tree with each commit, because each checkout makes or keeps its own copy of them, so where a commit holds such a file, as a commit of a build's output does, the working tree's copy need not match it.

The refusal names the files the push is refused for, because whether each is committed, removed or ignored is for whoever pushes to decide.

The consent that counts is the trust a user gives a folder in Claude Code, before which a plugin the project declares does not load; a repository taking the method runs its own code at every push anyway, since the pre-push hook runs its tests; and the case left open needs together the plugin installed by the user rather than declared by the project, Claude Code run without its dialog of trust, and a clone nobody looked at.

decisions.ruling: The owner: it waits past the first release, 0.1.0, and the todo stays. The export and the map are views kept in the working tree, which git does not keep and no check reads, and they lag only until the next edit or commit.

children.title: The schema and a project's extension
children.text:
`sheriff validate` validates each file with a JSON Schema validator against the base schema of the SpecSheriff guidelines, composed with the project's extension (§s-eferktypcj7njt5).

The extension is validated first, against the schema of an extension. That schema lets an extension add only kinds, fields of an existing kind, and properties of a file or of a link.

What the extension adds joins the base schema:

- its kinds join the kinds a node may have;
- its conditions join those every node is held to;
- its properties of a file and of a link join those a file and a link may hold.

`sheriff binding` validates each file against the same schema before it checks anything.

`sheriff reindex` validates each file once it has merged each key written twice and changed what an earlier release wrote, as §s-f5rz6b7dhxejjts says, and before it computes anything. It leaves out of that validation only what it writes itself:

- the links pointing at a node;
- outside the archive, a sid a node lacks, every location, a header's index of its sections and the values gathered beside a field.

Where the schema refuses a file, or the schema of an extension refuses the project's extension, each of the two commands names that file or the extension and every refusal in it. It then checks nothing more, and `sheriff reindex` writes no file.
children.reason: Each command is written for the shape the schema gives a file. Only a validation against the schema names where a file departs from that shape and what is wrong there. `sheriff reindex` builds each file from all of them, so writing only some would leave the files disagreeing with one another. A key written twice is merged first, since a file read without the merge holds only its last value. What an earlier release wrote is changed first, since the schema refuses its old names. What `sheriff reindex` writes itself is left out, since a node written by hand lacks it until the command runs.

children.title: Checks made by `sheriff binding`
children.text: How `sheriff binding` makes each of its checks.

children.title: The symbols a commit changes
children.text:
`sheriff binding` finds which symbols of the system's code the commit changes.

- A changed line counts for the symbol it stands in. A change anywhere in a symbol is a change of the whole symbol.
- A line holding a tag, before the commit or after it, counts for the symbol the tag marks, even where it stands outside the symbol's body.

A symbol does not count as changed where each of its changed lines:

- is not a line holding a tag;
- differs from the line it replaces only in a comment, in the sid a citation names, or in an identifier the commit renames throughout.

children.title: Tags on the system's code
children.text:
A tag links a symbol to the node the symbol implements. `sheriff binding` reads the tag of every symbol of the system's code. The system's code is the code that implements the specification, its tests included.

- The tests carry sids rather than tags (§s-utf4mbt7ref8g9c), so their symbols are not read.
- The repository's configuration, its own tools and their tests are not the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc), and are not read.
- An inner symbol is covered by the tag of the symbol it stands in.
- The sid of a tag is looked up among the nodes, and that of a tag on a changed symbol among the checked ones. A symbol changes where a line the commit changes counts for it (§s-2x58az67bm6cxq2).
- While the specification is in draft mode (§s-j9r8z4xdrfkfs47), a symbol carrying no tag that the commit does not change is reported by the symbol, not refused (§s-kkbqcb9xrpaepwn).

decisions.problem: The system's code came to include its tests, which carry a sid rather than a tag.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-hheus6f395ynqvc: the repository's configuration, its own tools and their tests are not the system's code.

children.title: From draft mode to live mode
children.text:
`sheriff binding` lets a commit take the specification from draft mode to live mode only once it is ready, and never back (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2).

- The specification is in draft mode until `project.json` holds the rule that puts it live, and in live mode after.
- In draft mode, a symbol without a tag that a commit does not change is reported rather than refused (§s-kkbqcb9xrpaepwn). In live mode, it is refused.

A commit adding that rule is refused unless both of these hold:

- the rule is checked in the commit;
- every symbol of the system's code but its tests carries a tag.

A commit taking that rule out of `project.json` is refused.

children.title: The tag that binds a symbol to its rule
children.text:
A tag is the line `@spec <sid>` in the comment directly above the symbol it binds, above its decorators where it has any — in TypeScript and JavaScript its doc comment, in Python a comment line — and a symbol implementing several rules carries several.

A symbol that implements no rule says so with `@spec none`, followed by the reason it carries none, and one standing first in a run of re-exports, with no blank line between them, says it for the whole run.

The delimiters of the comment may share a tag's line and nothing else may, so that a tag's text is found by a scan in any language. Which symbol a tag stands on is found by parsing the file with tree-sitter and the grammar of the file's language — the parser alone, with no program and no type checker — and a description of each language names what counts as a declaration and as a test in it; TypeScript, JavaScript and Python are described.
children.reason: A comment above a symbol is where an editor shows a tag and where a reader of the symbol is already looking. A scan finds a tag but cannot see what it is attached to, so a tag standing over nothing would pass it; the parser sees the symbol under the comment, and used alone it answers the same for the same file every time and is cheap enough to run at every commit. One parser with a grammar per language makes a further language a description rather than new code.

decisions.problem: The tag's rule says a tag stands in the doc comment above the symbol it binds, and nothing checked it: the check read tags by scanning, which finds a tag and can say nothing about what it is attached to. A tag naming a rule and standing over a blank line, or trailing a statement, passed. For the same reason the symbols a node names in its metadata were not graded at all, only the files.
decisions.ruling: Where a tag stands is decided by parsing the file — the parser only, no program and no type checker. A tag binds to the declaration below it where no blank line separates them, and a node that names symbols is held to the ones its tags stand on. A language server was refused for the same job: its answer depends on the state of a running server, and the checks require the same commit to get the same answer every time (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh).

decisions.ruling: The owner: the exemption stands on the declaration, and on the first of a run of re-exports for the whole run.

decisions.ruling: The owner: one general parser, with a grammar per language, reads the code; a language is added by describing what counts as a declaration and as a test in it, and TypeScript, JavaScript and Python are described at launch.

children.title: Who runs the reviewer
children.reason:
Print mode and `codex exec` answer once and exit, with no session around them to carry anything over. How a runner is started keeps from it everything of the session that wrote the code, so that it judges the code against the nodes alone, not against what its author meant.

A CLI held to the schema of the verdict answers in a form `sheriff review` can read. An answer that contradicts itself leaves open which half the reviewer meant, and taking either would decide for it.

A command script runs only through a shell, so the program it starts is started instead. A shell in between reads the arguments by rules of its own. On Windows, ending that shell at the time limit leaves the CLI it started running.

The environment lists what passes, since a list of what to strip would fall behind unseen. An agent sets variables of its own for the session it runs, and a new release may add more. The git hooks set git's variables to the repository, which a CLI started in its empty directory would then read through them. A variable the run needs, left off the list, fails the run instead, and the commit is refused saying why.

A run of the reviewer is paid for by the user who commits, from their own account. So it runs at the models and the efforts that user has confirmed, kept on their machine rather than in the project, which every clone shares. The git hooks read the git configuration with no agent running, and it outlives an update or a removal of either plugin. Its global scope serves every project of the user, so one answer on each machine holds wherever they commit. A confirmed setting holds its value, so that a release of the SpecSheriff tools offering other defaults changes nothing a user has confirmed.

Where a setting is not confirmed, the review still runs at its default. A commit whose review cannot be held is refused (§s-nyh9yk22ba6g77q). Refusing would then hold every commit of a user nobody has asked yet, as one committing from a terminal or in CI. The default is named with every review it runs, so that nobody pays long without knowing at what.

Whether code does only what its rules say is the one judgement among the checks, so it is asked at high effort. With Codex, high was the lowest effort tried at which the reviewer refused, in every run, a change it must refuse. At lower efforts it passed that change in some runs or in all. Nothing was measured with Claude, whose runner is asked the same effort so that the two runners judge alike. The default of the runner `claude` is `opus`, the model Anthropic names as its default, rather than its most capable model. That model costs the user more for each review. The runner falls back to `sonnet` so that a review is held where `opus` is overloaded or not offered. Which models Codex offers depends on how its user signs in, so the default of the runner `codex` is the one Codex chooses for that account. Codex offers no run without tools, so its runner turns off every one a setting reaches, and its sandbox lets nothing be written.

The runner follows the plugin a user has, since a user with one agent has no other to run. A project wanting one reviewer for everyone names it. The limit on a run's time is long, since it ends a run that hangs rather than hurrying one that reads a large change.

children.title: How a confirmation is recorded
children.text:
`sheriff confirm <sid>...` appends to `specs/_confirmations.jsonl` one line per node — its sid, the fingerprint of its wording and the owner confirming it, who is the email git is configured with — and sets the node's status to checked. It refuses a node whose owner is someone else, naming that owner, and appends nothing for a node where the latest line for that fingerprint is already a confirmation by its owner.

`sheriff confirm --withdraw <sid>...`, which anyone may run, appends a line withdrawing the confirmation of the wording the node holds, naming as `by` whoever withdraws it, the email git is configured with, and empties its status. Of the lines for one fingerprint, the latest decides.

The fingerprint is a SHA-256 hash of one canonical string holding the node's title, text and reason and the values its kind carries beside them, but neither the owner a node names nor what the reindex builds, the keys of an object sorted and a list in its own order. In that string the reason stands under the key `rationale`, the name earlier releases gave it. Earlier releases gave a field of type one of an empty list of its own values where the domains add its values. In that string such a field stands in that form. An owner is named by an email.
children.reason: One line appended per confirmation merges between branches without a conflict and keeps every confirmation ever given, and with the latest line deciding, a withdrawal cannot be undone by typing a status back. SHA-256 is a hash every language provides. The email git is configured with is the one a commit names its author by, so a confirmation and the commit carrying it name the same person. The owner a node names says who reads its wording, not what the wording is, and what the reindex builds is no one's wording. A fingerprint changes with the name and value of every key in its string. A release writing the wording in another form would otherwise empty the status of every node confirmed before it, though no wording changed.

decisions.problem: Confirmations were kept in one person's files outside the repository, guarded by that person's hooks, so nobody else could check a status and a lost file would have emptied every status.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a confirmation is kept with the specification, names who gave it and is accepted only under that owner's signature.

decisions.problem: The line withdrawing a confirmation named whoever withdrew it as its owner, though anyone may withdraw one.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's ruling on §s-5ah25f6gy99panq: anyone runs the withdrawal, and its line names whoever withdraws it as by.

decisions.problem: The owner renamed a node's id to location, its rationale to reason and the kind record to RecordType, while every project's files and confirmations hold the old names.
decisions.ruling: A technical consequence in the owner's name: the reason keeps its old label in the fingerprint, so no confirmation is lost.

decisions.problem: The reindex rewrites an earlier release's empty own list of a field of type one of into the source the domains add, which changed the fingerprint: every RecordType confirmed with such a field would lose its confirmation at the first reindex after an upgrade.
decisions.ruling: The owner: such a field stands in the fingerprint's string as earlier releases wrote it, as the reason stands under its earlier name.

children.title: A git hook runs the SpecSheriff tools a plugin keeps on the machine
children.text:
When a session starts, the plugin for Claude Code (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5) copies the SpecSheriff tools it carries into its data directory, `<plugins>/data/specsheriff-specsheriff-marketplace/`, where the copy there is of another release or missing; `<plugins>` is `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR` where it is set and `~/.claude/plugins` otherwise. The plugin for Codex CLI (§s-2pdy9gw2jrjvfb4) keeps no copy: its tools stand in its directory in Codex's cache, `<Codex home>/plugins/cache/specsheriff-marketplace/specsheriff/<version>/tools/`, where `<Codex home>` is `CODEX_HOME` where it is set and `~/.codex` otherwise. `~` is the user's home directory, on Windows their profile directory.

Each git hook `sheriff init` writes holds the lookup of those tools, a call to the script for that hook in their `hooks/`, what it does where it finds none, and the run of the project's own tools (§s-n4m5zvh96yb299p). Where it finds the tools of both plugins, it takes those whose `release` file opens with the higher version, compared as semantic versions, and either where the two are equal. The script runs what the hook is to run (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw), and refuses where Node is missing or older than the tools need, naming the version they need.

Where the hook finds the tools of neither plugin, it runs the project's own tools (§s-n4m5zvh96yb299p) and lets the commit or the push through unless one of them fails. The pre-commit and pre-push hooks say then that no check of SpecSheriff ran, because they found the SpecSheriff tools of no plugin on the machine.

The script run when a session starts names each git hook in `.githooks/`, and each of the agent's hooks for Codex in `.codex/hooks.json`, that holds what an earlier release of `sheriff init` wrote, and says that `sheriff init` replaces it (§s-7unxytshhc4md54).
children.reason:
Claude Code keeps each version of a plugin in a directory of its own, which changes with every update, and keeps the plugin's data directory across updates; so the plugin keeps a copy of its release there, at a path a hook written once can name. Codex keeps the one installed version of a plugin in its cache and deletes the cache when the plugin is removed, while it leaves the plugin's data directory; a copy kept there would outlive the plugin, so the hook looks in the cache, which goes with it.

The hook looks for the tools of both plugins because a user may move from one agent to the other, and takes the higher release because it holds every fix of the lower.

A hook that finds no tools is most often one whose user removed the plugin. Refusing would hold every commit of that user while checking nothing, so the hook lets it through and says so. The hooks stay on so that the project's own tools keep running, so the notice recurs at every commit and push. Where the tools are found but cannot run, the plugin is there and its user expects the checks to hold, so the script refuses.

A hook is a file of the project, which only a commit changes, so a hook written by an earlier release keeps its lookup until `sheriff init` replaces it; the session start says so, because it runs in every clone.

children.title: The project's own tools in a git hook
children.text:
Each git hook `sheriff init` writes runs the project's own tools for it after the checks of the SpecSheriff tools (§s-pcnyfp7gev7syax). They are the files directly in `.githooks/<hook>.d/` whose first line names their interpreter, run in the byte order of their names. A first line names an interpreter where it opens with `#!`, followed by a path and at most one argument, a closing carriage return left out. The hook names each other file there and does not run it.

The hook runs them whatever the checks found, the script refusing where Node is missing or too old included, and also where it finds no SpecSheriff tools (§s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p). Each of the project's tools:

- runs from the root of the working tree, by the interpreter its first line names, in git's own environment, so it reads the working tree and git's index;
- is handed the arguments git hands the hook and a copy of the standard input git hands it.

Each of them runs, whatever the others find. The hook fails where the checks refuse or one of the project's tools ends with an exit status other than zero, naming each such tool. It fails too where one of them changes the staged files or the commit's message, naming it.

These files are among the repository's own tools, not the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc).
children.reason: A repository taking up the method has its hooks in `.githooks/`, which `core.hooksPath` names, so git runs the project's own tools nowhere else. Kept in a folder of their own, they are the project's files, which `sheriff init` neither replaces nor names as changed by hand. Each of them runs, so that each reports what it would report alone. One is chosen by its first line rather than by the executable bit, which a file committed from a system keeping none loses. The pre-push hook's input names the refs pushed, which a tool judging a push needs as the hook does.

decisions.problem: The project's own tools needed a way to be registered that a hook can read even where no SpecSheriff tools are on the machine.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project registers its own tools for a hook by placing them in .githooks/<hook>.d/, which the hook reads at every run, rather than by a list in sheriff.config.json, which a hook without the SpecSheriff tools could not read; sheriff init neither knows nor registers them.

children.title: The plugin for Claude Code carries everything its work needs
children.text:

children.title: What a RecordType generates
children.text:
From each RecordType, `sheriff types` writes a type into each file of types and a definition under `$defs` into each file of runtime checks. It takes the nodes in the order the specification reads: its files in the code-point order of their paths, and the nodes of each file in the order they stand.

Every type and definition is named by the RecordType's name with the first letter of each word raised and the spaces dropped. Each type is tagged with the sid of its RecordType, as a symbol of code is tagged with the rule it implements (§s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp).

A type and a definition hold the fields of every RecordType above the node along its refines links, the topmost first, then the node's own fields, except a variant's own, which stand where the rule on RecordType variants places them (§s-nk8td3ez58gahc4); each field keeps its name and the order its node gives it, and is required where its node says so and optional otherwise. A field of type record refers to the type of that RecordType by its name, and the object of a field of type variant is written out in full. Where the RecordType refuses a field nobody declared, its definition refuses any property its fields do not declare.

A name that is not an identifier in the language of its file, or that the file already uses — the names it imports and those its language builds in included — cannot be generated.

In TypeScript a type is written `export type <name> = {...}`.

In Python a type is written `<name> = TypedDict("<name>", {...})`, every name it uses imported from `typing`, a reference to another type written as a string, an optional field marked `NotRequired`, and the object of a field of type variant given a type of its own, named by the type it stands in followed by the field's name with its first letter raised, and tagged with the same sid.
children.reason:
One name in every file lets a reader follow a RecordType from its node to each copy, and a fixed order makes each file come out the same at every run, which the comparison of generated copies needs. The generator writes the tag itself, so that the link from each type to its node is made anew with the type and never kept by hand.

A RecordType that refines another holds that one's fields, as the schema of the nodes says, and a field keeps the name its node gives because the code uses that name as it stands. Only a runtime check can refuse an undeclared property; a type in TypeScript or Python cannot.

A name the file already uses would break its compilation or hide what it imports.

The functional form of `TypedDict` takes any field name, a keyword of Python included; a reference written as a string may name a type written later in the file, or the type itself; and Python can name the object of a field only by a type of its own.

children.title: A RecordType its variants refine
children.text:
A RecordType that variants refine — RecordTypes each answering to values of its choosing fields, the fields whose values choose which variant a RecordType is — is written as the union of its members: in JSON Schema a definition holding `oneOf` the members, in TypeScript a union type, in Python `<name> = Union[...]`. Its members are each variant, referred to by the name of its type, and, where some combination of the choosing fields' values has no variant, a member for those combinations, named by the RecordType's name followed by `Other`: a type and a definition of their own, the type tagged with the RecordType's sid.

A variant holds each choosing field, required and fixed to the value it answers to, and its own fields inside the RecordType's field of type variant, beside the fields that field holds, or, where the RecordType has no such field, beside the RecordType's fields; the variant's node decides whether a property nobody declared is refused there and around it.

The member for the other combinations holds the RecordType's fields, its choosing fields required where their node says so. Its definition refuses every combination of values a variant answers to; its type gives a choosing field the values no variant answers to where one field chooses, and all its values where several do; the RecordType's node decides whether a property nobody declared is refused.

A field of type variant is required where its object holds a field and is not declared otherwise, whether or not variants refine its RecordType.
children.reason:
A union whose members the choosing fields tell apart is how JSON Schema, TypeScript and Python each state that a RecordType's fields depend on its values, and with the choosing fields required in every variant at most one member matches. A value that brings no fields of its own has no variant, as the rule on variants says (§s-z3dnru6qqdf9m6j), so the RecordType itself answers for it, under a name its own name gives and with its own tag.

Each member follows its own node on undeclared properties, so that no node's setting overrides another's. A runtime check can refuse every combination of values a variant claims; a type can name only the values each field holds, which is exact where one field chooses.

An object with no field in it holds nothing, so the field for it is not declared.

children.title: The type each neutral type of a field gives
children.text:
Each neutral type a field may have gives, in a file of runtime checks and in a file of types, what the table below says.

A field of type one of gives the values of its own list, in its order. Where its values come from elsewhere, it gives those gathered beside it (§s-ju5vcanbjph7mgh), in this order:

- by the node each comes from, the files of the specification in the code-point order of their paths and the nodes of a file in the order they stand;
- the members of one list in their order.

| Field's type | JSON Schema | TypeScript | Python |
|---|---|---|---|
| text | `{"type": "string"}` | `string` | `str` |
| email address | `{"type": "string", "format": "email"}` | `string` | `str` |
| whole number | `{"type": "integer"}`, with its bounds | `number` | `int` |
| number | `{"type": "number"}`, with its bounds | `number` | `float` |
| yes/no | `{"type": "boolean"}` | `boolean` | `bool` |
| instant | `{"type": "string", "format": "date-time"}` | `string` | `str` |
| date | `{"type": "string", "format": "date"}` | `string` | `str` |
| duration | `{"type": "string", "format": "duration"}` | `string` | `str` |
| any value | `{}` | `unknown` | `Any` |
| one of | `{"enum": [<its values>]}` | the union of its values as literals | `Literal[<its values>]` |
| list of | `{"type": "array", "items": <its members' type>}`, with its bounds on how many members it holds | `<its members' type>[]` | `list[<its members' type>]` |
| map of | `{"type": "object", "additionalProperties": <its values' type>}` | `Record<string, <its values' type>>` | `dict[str, <its values' type>]` |
| record | `{"$ref": "#/$defs/<its type's name>"}` | its type's name | its type's name, as a string |
| identifier of | what the field identifying that RecordType gives | what that field gives | what that field gives |
| variant | an object holding its fields | an object holding its fields | its own type |
children.reason:
JSON Schema is the standard every language has a validator for, and the bounds on a number's value and on how many members a field of type list of holds are already named in the nodes as JSON Schema names them. Each language's own type for a value is the one its code reads without a conversion: an instant, a date and a duration travel as text, each in the form of ISO 8601 its `format` names. A bound is carried by the runtime checks alone, which run alike in every language. A type in Python can state none. An identifier has the type of the field that identifies the RecordType it names, so that a value moving from that field to a field referring to it keeps its type and passes the same check.

The generator reads a field's values in one place, whatever their source. `sheriff validate` already compares the gathered values with their source (§s-agc6fb3vx46pc23), so the generator collects nothing again. A fixed order makes each file come out the same at every run, which the comparison of generated copies needs.
